name: French
note: Spelling and sound part ways in French: the Alphabet card lists the pairings

alphabet.e: lips rounded for oo while the tongue holds ee: tu, rue
oo as in soup: vous, jour
wa as in watt: trois, noir
the vowel of her, lips rounded: deux, sœur
e as in bed: lait, neige
o as in note: chaud, bateau
nasal o, the n itself is not sounded: bonjour
nasal a, the n itself is not sounded: grand
nasal e, the n itself is not sounded: vin, pain
nasal eu, heard in un and lundi
closed e in café, open e in père
sh as in ship: chat, chercher
ny as in canyon: montagne, gagner
s as in measure: jour, rouge
y as in yes: fille, travailler
scraped at the back of the throat, never rolled: rue

alphabet.c: final d p s t x z
alphabet.e: silent at the end of a word: petit, vous, nez

units.title: BASICS
units.subtitle: Greeting people, naming who is who, and counting to twelve

tips.h: Bonjour and the time of day
tips.b: French greets by the part of the day. Bonjour serves from morning until dusk, bonsoir replaces it after dark, and bonne nuit is said only when parting for the night. Salut works in both directions, arriving and leaving, and only among people on familiar terms.
A greeting to a stranger carries a title: bonjour madame, bonjour monsieur. Leaving the title out is short to the point of rudeness in a shop or an office.

phrases.e: Good evening madam, all is well

tips.b: French has two words where English has one you. Tu addresses one friend, one relative or one child. Vous addresses a stranger, an older person, anyone in a position of authority, and any group of two or more. The verb ending changes with the choice.
Ils stands for a group of men and for any mixed group. Elles is used only when every member of the group is female. One man in a group of a hundred women makes the whole group ils.
Spoken French replaces nous with on for we. On takes the same verb form as il and elle, so the verb looks singular while the meaning is plural.
The polite please is s'il vous plaît, built on vous. With someone addressed as tu it becomes s'il te plaît. Both mean if it pleases, with vous or te naming the person addressed.
Très modifies an adjective or an adverb, beaucoup modifies a verb or a quantity. The two are never stacked: très beaucoup does not exist.

phrases.e: Thank you very much and goodbye

phrases.ipa: ɛks.ky.ze mwa mə.sjø sil vu plɛ

tips.b: Cinq, six, huit and dix sound their final consonant when counting or standing alone. Before a noun beginning with a consonant that ending falls silent, and before a vowel it links across as a z or a t.
Un means one and is also the masculine word for a. The feminine pair is une. The sentence, not the word, separates the number from the article.
Age uses avoir rather than être: j'ai dix ans. The word ans is part of the expression and is never dropped the way years is in English.

phrases.e: The boy is six years old

units.title: EVERYDAY
units.subtitle: Food, drink, colour and the people of a household

tips.b: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article marks which one: le pain, la pomme. The ending is only a weak clue, so the gender is listed beside each noun in this course and is worth learning as part of the word.

tips.h: The partitive du, de la, des
tips.b: An unmeasured quantity of something takes a partitive article: du before a masculine noun, de la before a feminine one, de l' before a vowel, and des before a plural. English drops the article here; French does not.
Hunger and thirst are things a person has in French, not things a person is. Avoir faim is to be hungry and avoir soif is to be thirsty, and the noun takes no article.
A container and its contents are joined by de with no article between them: un verre de vin, une tasse de café, une bouteille d'eau.

phrases.t: Un verre de vin, s'il vous plaît
phrases.ipa: œ̃ vɛʁ də vɛ̃ sil vu plɛ

tips.b: A colour adjective is placed after the noun it describes: une pomme rouge, un chapeau noir. English puts the colour first; French almost never does.

An adjective takes the gender and the number of its noun. Most add -e for the feminine and -s for the plural: vert, verte, verts, vertes. An adjective already ending in -e, such as rouge or jaune, keeps one form in both genders.
Marron and orange are nouns pressed into service as adjectives and keep a single form: des chaussures marron, des murs orange.

A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. Mon goes before a masculine noun, ma before a feminine one, mes before any plural. Ton and son, votre and leur follow the same rule, so son père is his father or her father depending on who is speaking.
Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel sound, ma is replaced by mon: mon amie, mon école. The gender of the noun is unchanged, only the sound of the pair.
Possession between two nouns is built with de, and the owned thing comes first: la fille de Marie is Marie's daughter. There is no apostrophe-s in French.

units.title: ACTIONS
units.subtitle: The present tense, describing, asking a question and denying

tips.b: Most French verbs end in -er. Removing that ending leaves a stem, and the stem takes -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Four of the six endings are silent, so je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent all sound alike; only nous and vous stand apart by ear.
The two most used verbs follow no pattern and are learned as blocks. Être: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. Avoir: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont.
Je parle covers both I speak and I am speaking. French has no separate continuous form, so the context carries that difference.

tips.h: Adjectives that go before the noun
tips.b: The default position is after the noun, but a short closed set comes before it: beau, bon, grand, gros, jeune, joli, mauvais, nouveau, petit, vieux. Most of these describe size, age, beauty or worth.

tips.h: Beau, nouveau, vieux and a vowel
tips.b: Three of those adjectives take a separate masculine form before a vowel sound: bel, nouvel, vieil. Their feminine forms are belle, nouvelle and vieille.
An adjective in -eux forms its feminine in -euse, one in -f forms it in -ve, and several double the final consonant before the -e: bon becomes bonne, gros becomes grosse.

Rising intonation alone turns a statement into a question in speech: tu parles français. Est-ce que placed in front of an unchanged statement does the same in any register. Inversion of verb and pronoun is the formal and written form: parles-tu français.
A question word opens the sentence and is followed either by est-ce que or by an inversion: où est-ce que tu habites, où habites-tu. In casual speech it can also be left at the end: tu habites où.
Quel is a determiner rather than a pronoun and takes the gender and number of the noun after it: quel livre, quelle fille, quels livres, quelles filles. All four forms sound the same.

phrases.e: How many brothers do you have?

tips.b: A negative sentence puts ne in front of the verb and pas after it: je ne parle pas. Ne shortens to n' before a vowel sound. In relaxed speech the ne is often dropped and pas alone carries the negation.
Jamais, rien, personne and plus take the place of pas instead of joining it. The ne stays: je ne mange rien, il ne vient jamais, elle ne travaille plus.
The partitive du, de la and des collapse to de after a negation: j'ai du pain becomes je n'ai pas de pain. Un and une do the same: j'ai un frère becomes je n'ai pas de frère.

phrases.t: Elle ne mange jamais de viande
phrases.ipa: ɛl nə mɑ̃ʒ ʒa.mɛ də vjɑ̃d

units.title: AT HOME
units.subtitle: The house, the things in it, clothing and animals

tips.h: Il y a for there is
tips.b: Il y a covers both there is and there are, and the form never changes with number. Its negative is il n'y a pas, and the partitive after it becomes de.
eg: Il n'y a pas de jardin.

tips.b: Position is stated with a preposition and the ordinary article: dans places a thing inside, sur on top, sous underneath. None of the three contracts with le on its own.
The preposition à contracts with the definite article: à plus le gives au, à plus les gives aux. À la and à l' stay as two words.

phrases.t: Le chat est dans le jardin
phrases.e: The cat is in the garden
phrases.ipa: lə ʃa ɛ dɑ̃ lə ʒaʁ.dɛ̃

tips.b: The indefinite article is un before a masculine noun, une before a feminine one, and des before any plural. English has no plural article at all, while French requires des.

This and that are one word in French. Ce stands before a masculine noun, cet before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel sound, cette before a feminine noun, and ces before any plural. Adding -ci or -là after the noun marks near from far.

phrases.t: Le livre est sur le lit
phrases.e: The book is on the bed
phrases.ipa: lə livʁ ɛ syʁ lə li

tips.b: Porter is used both for wearing a garment and for carrying an object, and the context separates them. It is a regular -er verb: je porte, tu portes, nous portons.
Most nouns add a silent -s in the plural. Nouns ending in -eau add -x instead, also silent: un manteau, des manteaux. The article carries the number to the ear.

phrases.e: She is wearing a red dress

phrases.t: Il ne porte pas de chapeau
phrases.e: He is not wearing a hat
phrases.ipa: il nə pɔʁt pa də ʃa.po

tips.b: A noun ending in -al forms its plural in -aux, and the change is heard as well as written: un cheval, des chevaux; un animal, des animaux.

The gender of an animal noun belongs to the word, not to the creature: la souris is feminine whatever mouse it names. A few common animals do have a feminine partner: le chien and la chienne, le chat and la chatte.

units.title: TIME
units.subtitle: The calendar, the clock and the weather

tips.h: Days are written in lower case
tips.b: French writes lundi and mardi without a capital. A day with le in front of it names a habit: le lundi means on Mondays, while lundi on its own means this coming Monday.
A French week runs from lundi to dimanche, so dimanche closes it rather than opening it. Le week-end names samedi and dimanche together.

phrases.e: Tomorrow I am going to Paris

tips.b: In January is en janvier, with no article between the preposition and the month. Au mois de janvier is the longer form and means the same thing.
A date takes an ordinary number and the definite article, with the day before the month: le deux mars. The one exception is the first of the month, which takes le premier.
The hour is given with il est and the word heure or heures. Minutes past are added straight after, minutes to use moins. Et quart names the quarter hour and et demie the half hour.
eg: Il est deux heures et quart.
It is a quarter past two.
Il est six heures et demie.
Il est huit heures moins cinq.

tips.b: Timetables use the twenty-four hour clock: le train de dix-huit heures. Speech uses the twelve hour clock and adds the part of the day: six heures du soir.
A part of the day with le in front of it states a habit: le matin je bois du café. Ce matin points at the morning of today.
Most statements about the weather use the impersonal il fait followed by an adjective: il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait beau. The il stands for nothing at all.
Rain and snow have impersonal verbs of their own: il pleut, il neige. Wind and sun are stated with il y a and a partitive: il y a du vent, il y a du soleil.

phrases.e: It is raining a lot today

units.title: GETTING AROUND
units.subtitle: Places in town, directions, transport and travel

tips.h: Au, à la and à l'
tips.b: À covers both at and to, so je vais à la gare and je suis à la gare use the same preposition. It contracts with le to make au and with les to make aux, and stays apart before la and before a vowel.
De marks origin and belonging, and contracts the same way: de plus le gives du, de plus les gives des. Before a vowel it becomes d'.

phrases.e: I am going to the bank
The school is on this street

phrases.t: Le marché est près de l'église
phrases.e: The market is near the church
phrases.ipa: lə maʁ.ʃe ɛ pʁɛ də le.ɡliz

tips.b: A place is asked for with où est or où sont. A direction is given with à gauche, à droite or tout droit, and tout droit means straight ahead rather than to the right.
Près and loin take de before the place they measure from: près de la gare, loin de la ville. That de contracts with le and les as usual, giving près du parc and loin des magasins.

phrases.e: The bank is on the right

phrases.t: Le chat est sous la chaise
phrases.e: The cat is under the chair
phrases.ipa: lə ʃa ɛ su la ʃɛz

phrases.e: My house is far from here

phrases.t: Le parc est entre deux rues
phrases.e: The park is between two streets

tips.b: A vehicle one sits inside takes en: en voiture, en train, en avion. A vehicle one sits on takes à, and so does travelling on foot: à vélo, à moto, à pied.
The verb for using a service is prendre: je prends le bus. Its present is irregular: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent.

phrases.e: I am taking the train tomorrow

phrases.t: Nous allons à l'école en autobus
phrases.e: We go to school by bus

tips.b: Aller is irregular and is worth learning whole: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. On its own it means to go, and with à it names a destination.
Aller followed by an infinitive states what is about to happen: je vais partir. Only aller is conjugated; the second verb keeps its dictionary form. This is the ordinary spoken future.
eg: We are going to visit Paris.
He is going to arrive tomorrow.

tips.b: Being on holiday is en vacances. Vacances is plural in this sense and has no singular, so the adjective and the article are plural too.

phrases.e: I am going to visit Paris

phrases.t: Mon train part à huit heures

phrases.e: We are waiting at the airport

units.title: PEOPLE
units.subtitle: Feelings, the body, health and describing a person

tips.b: Several states are had rather than felt in French: avoir peur, avoir honte, avoir raison. The noun follows avoir with no article, and de introduces whatever caused the feeling.

A reflexive verb carries a pronoun that matches its subject and stands before the verb: je me sens, tu te sens, il se sent, nous nous sentons, vous vous sentez, ils se sentent. The dictionary form keeps se in front.

An adjective describing a person takes that person's gender and number: il est content, elle est contente, ils sont contents, elles sont contentes. Only the written form changes for content; for heureux the sound changes too.

phrases.t: Mon frère a peur des chiens
phrases.e: My brother is afraid of dogs
phrases.ipa: mɔ̃ fʁɛʁ a pœʁ de ʃjɛ̃
phrases.lit: my brother has fear of-the dogs

tips.h: The body takes le, la and les
tips.b: A body part is named with the definite article where English uses a possessive, because the owner is already clear from the verb or the pronoun: il lève la main, elle ferme les yeux, je me lave les mains.
Œil has an unrelated plural, yeux. Cheveux names a whole head of hair and is used in the plural; un cheveu is one single strand.

phrases.lit: I have pain to the head

tips.b: A pain is stated with avoir mal à followed by the body part, and that à contracts as usual: avoir mal au dos, avoir mal à la jambe, avoir mal aux dents.
eg: Elle a mal à la main.

tips.b: Illness is stated with être malade. General wellbeing uses aller: je vais bien, il va mal. The everyday question ça va asks about the same thing.
Chez names a person's home or a professional's premises: chez moi, chez le médecin, chez le boulanger. It is used with a person, never with the name of a town.

phrases.e: He is going to the doctor

tips.b: A description of a person is built on être plus an adjective, and the adjective agrees: il est gentil, elle est gentille. Gentil doubles its l in the feminine, and the l is then heard.
More is plus, less is moins, and as is aussi, each followed by que before the thing compared. Bon has its own comparative, meilleur, and plus bon is not used.

phrases.t: Elle est plus grande que moi

units.title: WORK AND SCHOOL
units.subtitle: School, jobs, numbers past ten and money

tips.b: Many role nouns build a feminine: un étudiant becomes une étudiante, un boulanger becomes une boulangère. Un élève keeps its spelling and changes only its article, and professeur now has the written feminine professeure.
Apprendre and comprendre are built on prendre and take its endings: j'apprends, tu apprends, il apprend, nous apprenons, vous apprenez, ils apprennent.
The plural possessives are notre, votre and leur for one thing owned, and nos, vos and leurs for several. None of them changes with the gender of the noun.

phrases.e: The teacher writes on the board

tips.h: A job takes no article after être
tips.b: After être the name of a job stands bare: il est boulanger, elle est médecin. With c'est an article is required instead: c'est un boulanger.
Travail is the noun for work and travailler the verb. The plural of travail is travaux, which also names building works.

phrases.t: La réunion est à neuf heures

tips.b: French counts past sixty by addition. Soixante-dix is sixty-ten, quatre-vingts is four-twenties, and quatre-vingt-dix is four-twenties-ten. The pattern runs on: soixante-douze is seventy-two and quatre-vingt-quinze is ninety-five.
Units are joined to tens with a hyphen, except one, which takes et and no hyphen: vingt et un, trente et un, soixante et onze. Quatre-vingt-un breaks the pattern and keeps the hyphen.
Cent takes an -s when it is multiplied and nothing follows it: deux cents, but deux cent cinq. Mille never takes an -s at all.
A price is asked for with combien: combien ça coûte, or c'est combien in speech. The answer uses coûter or faire, and faire is the commoner of the two at a till.
Argent names both the metal and money in general, and takes a partitive: j'ai de l'argent. A single coin is une pièce and a banknote is un billet.

phrases.e: How much does this book cost?
She spends a lot of money

units.title: OUT AND ABOUT
units.subtitle: Ordering, buying and what people do for pleasure

tips.b: An order is placed with je voudrais, a conditional form of vouloir that softens the request. Je veux is blunt to the point of rudeness in a shop or a restaurant.
The meals are le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner and le dîner. Déjeuner and dîner are verbs as well as nouns, so je déjeune à midi is an ordinary sentence.
The bill in a restaurant is l'addition, while une facture is the written invoice a business sends. Service is included by law, so a pourboire is an extra rather than an expectation.

phrases.e: I would like to order a dish

tips.b: A second regular group ends in -ir and inserts -iss- in the plural forms: je choisis, tu choisis, il choisit, nous choisissons, vous choisissez, ils choisissent. Finir and guérir follow the same pattern.
A shop is often the product plus -erie: pain gives boulangerie, viande gives boucherie. The person who keeps it takes -er in the masculine and -ère in the feminine.

phrases.t: J'achète du pain à la boulangerie
phrases.e: I buy bread at the bakery
phrases.ipa: ʒa.ʃɛt dy pɛ̃ a la bu.lɑ̃.ʒʁi

phrases.e: The shop assistant is very kind

tips.b: Jouer takes à before a game or a sport and de before a musical instrument, and both prepositions contract with the article as usual: jouer au football, jouer du piano, jouer de la guitare.
Liking an activity is aimer followed straight by the infinitive, with nothing between them: j'aime lire, elle aime danser. Préférer and détester work the same way.

phrases.e: I like reading in the evening

tips.b: Taking part in a sport uses faire de plus the partitive: faire du vélo, faire de la natation. A team game played with a ball takes jouer à instead: jouer au football.
A third regular group ends in -re and drops it before the endings: je perds, tu perds, il perd, nous perdons, vous perdez, ils perdent. Attendre, vendre and répondre follow it.

phrases.e: The players are at the stadium

units.title: THE WORLD
units.subtitle: Nature, the city, countries and a wider set of verbs

tips.b: Some endings lean one way: nouns in -age, -eau and -ment are usually masculine, and nouns in -tion, -té and -ette are usually feminine. La plage and l'eau run against the rule, which is why the article is worth learning with the word.

tips.h: Le for a whole class of thing
tips.b: French uses le, la or les where English uses no article at all for a general statement: j'aime la nature, les arbres sont verts. A bare plural noun is not possible.

phrases.t: Il y a des fleurs ici

tips.h: Le and la change the meaning
tips.b: A few nouns carry two genders and two meanings. Le tour is a turn or a circuit while la tour is a tower; le poste is a job or a set while la poste is the post office.

tips.h: Y stands in for a place
tips.b: Y replaces a place already named and stands in front of the verb: je vais à Paris becomes j'y vais. It is the same y that sits inside il y a.

phrases.t: Le musée est près du pont
phrases.e: The museum is near the bridge
phrases.ipa: lə my.ze ɛ pʁɛ dy pɔ̃

phrases.t: Il y a beaucoup de bruit
phrases.e: There is a lot of noise
We are going to the post office

tips.h: En, au and aux with countries
tips.b: A feminine country takes en, a masculine one au, and a plural one aux: en Espagne, au Japon, aux États-Unis. A country whose name ends in -e is feminine, with le Mexique and le Cambodge as the main exceptions.
A nationality used as an adjective and the name of a language are written in lower case: il est français, je parle espagnol. Naming a person of that nationality takes a capital: un Français.

phrases.e: She is going to Japan tomorrow

tips.b: These three are followed directly by an infinitive with no preposition between them: je veux partir, je peux venir, je dois travailler. All three are irregular: je veux, je peux, je dois.
Savoir covers a fact or a learned skill: je sais nager, je sais où il habite. Connaître covers acquaintance with a person or a place and is never followed by a clause: je connais Paris.

tips.h: Venir de for the recent past
tips.b: Venir de followed by an infinitive states what happened a moment ago: je viens de manger. The tense stays present while the meaning is past.

phrases.e: You have to close the door
